The Pacific imperial pigeon (Ducula pacifica) is a large frugivorous columbid distributed across the islands of the southwestern Pacific Ocean. Adults exhibit considerable sexual size dimorphism, with breeding females attaining a maximum body mass of approximately 395 grams [Wwi = approximately 395 grams], a value that reflects the substantial energetic demands of egg production and extended parental care in this insular species. Newly hatched chicks emerge from the incubated egg at a remarkably low initial body mass of around 25.7 grams [Ww0 = around 25.7 grams], a figure estimated from allometric relationships with related Patagioenas species and consistent with the altricial developmental pattern typical of arboreal pigeons. This modest neonatal investment is offset by prolonged bi-parental provisioning during the nestling phase, during which chicks grow rapidly under the sustained thermoregulatory conditions provided by brooding adults. Field observations on Rarotonga indicate that the age at hatching, from the onset of incubation, is 26 days [ab = 26 days] when measured at a mean nest temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], a thermal regime that balances embryonic development with the risk of desiccation in exposed canopy nests.

Following hatching, the nestling period is characterized by a critical developmental milestone when the chick achieves its first sustained flight and departs the nest. Fledging, defined as the time since birth at which the young bird leaves the nest site, occurs at 26 days [tx = 26 days] under the same elevated thermal conditions typical of the species' nesting microhabitat, 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], a comparatively short interval for a columbid of this body size. The rapid fledging schedule likely represents an adaptation to high nest predation pressure from introduced rats and native avian predators on small oceanic islands. After fledging, juveniles enter a prolonged period of nutritional dependence on their parents, gradually transitioning to independent foraging over the subsequent weeks. This post-fledging care phase is energetically costly for the adults but appears essential for the development of proficient fruit-handling skills required to process the large drupes and figs that constitute the bulk of the species' diet. The observed maturation trajectory from hatching to fledging proceeds without major interruptions under favorable food availability.

Sexual maturation in the Pacific imperial pigeon follows a predictable sequence after the fledgling stage. Puberty, marking the onset of gonadal development and the first production of viable gametes, is attained at 78 days since birth [tp = 78 days since birth] when maintained at a body temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], a value consistent with the metabolic demands of a tropical frugivore. This relatively early attainment of reproductive physiology contrasts with a substantially delayed expression of actual breeding behavior. The time since birth at first successful brood, representing the age at which an individual produces its first clutch that results in fledged young, is considerably longer at approximately 2.5 years [tR = approximately 2.5 years], again measured under thermal conditions of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This considerable lag between physiological puberty and effective first reproduction is a common pattern among long-lived tropical birds and is thought to reflect the time required to acquire a breeding territory, form a stable pair bond, and develop the foraging efficiency necessary to support reproductive effort.

Reproductive output in Ducula pacifica is notably constrained relative to many continental columbids. Females typically produce two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two eggs per clutch], although a single egg per clutch has been documented in a small number of nests on islands with abundant food resources. The maximum reproductive rate is limited by the frequency of nesting attempts; breeding pairs typically complete only one successful nesting cycle per year [F_R_i = one successful nesting cycle per year], resulting in a low annual reproductive output that is characteristic of island endemics. This slow reproductive schedule is linked to the extended incubation and brooding periods, as well as the reliance on ephemeral fruit crops that may vary markedly between seasons. The combination of a reduced number of eggs per nesting attempt and a low frequency of reproductive events per year imposes strong selective pressure on adult survival and longevity to maintain stable population sizes. Such life-history traits render the species particularly vulnerable to elevated rates of adult mortality from introduced predators or habitat degradation.

Lifespan estimates for the Pacific imperial pigeon suggest a maximum recorded longevity of approximately 16 years [am = approximately 16 years] under natural field conditions at a standard body temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], a value comparable to that reported for other large-bodied tropical columbids of similar adult mass. Basal metabolic rate, measured as resting oxygen consumption in post-absorptive adults during the inactive phase of the diel cycle, averages approximately 143 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = approximately 143 milliliters of oxygen per hour] at a thermoneutral body temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This relatively modest metabolic expenditure is consistent with the species' low-activity foraging strategy and frugivorous diet, which typically yields reduced metabolic costs compared to insectivorous or granivorous birds of comparable size. The interaction between low reproductive output, extended lifespan, and moderate metabolic rate positions D. pacifica as a classic slow-lived tropical species, adapted to the relatively stable but resource-limited environments of Pacific island ecosystems. Continued monitoring of these life-history parameters is essential for assessing population viability under ongoing anthropogenic pressures.
